newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanians clash with police over lost savings.
newsitem.headline: Albanians clash with police over lost savings.

text.p: Hundreds of protesters demanding their money back from a get-rich-quick pyramid scheme fought with Albanian riot police on Wednesday and some tried to storm the home of the failed scheme's owner, witnesses said.
Scheme manager Maksude Kademi, a 30-year-old Romany gypsy woman who stopped repayments to depositors in November, told a jeering crowd she had no money to give them.

"This was a pyramid scheme that failed. So you have no reason to (protest and) ask the state to give you money," Kademi, widely known as Sude, told a crowd of several thousand through a megaphone from her western Tirana flat.

"I asked for a credit today but I could not get it. I will keep trying," she added, drawing boos and whistles from demonstrators, some of whom tried to break a police cordon barring them from her home.
Pyramid schemes, offering returns of up to 200 percent over three months, have sprung up across the impoverished Balkan state since the fall of communism in 1990.

Earlier on Wednesday, about 500 demonstrators broke away from a crowd of 5,000 that had gathered outside Sude's home and set off to march two kilometres (just over a mile) to the capital's main Skanderbeg Square.
They hurled stones at around 50 police wielding batons who blocked their progress. Witnesses said some protesters were hurt in the ensuing scuffles and several arrests were made.

Another group of around 1,000 protesters managed to break through a thin police cordon on a main thoroughfare but police wielding truncheons dispersed them. Onlookers said many, including old women, were beaten and they saw young men with blood trickling down their faces.
The interior ministry disputed the size of the crowd and denied there had been any police violence.

"We want our money back. (President) Sali Berisha you are a thief. (Prime Minister Aleksander) Meksi you are a thief. Down with the dictatorship," the crowd chanted, directing much anger against the Balkan country's political leadership.
"First they stole our votes and now they are trying to steal our money," one woman said, accusing the ruling Democratic Party of failing to keep its election promises of security and prosperity.

The opposition Socialists slammed Berisha and his conservative Democratic Party and claimed they had turned a blind eye to the schemes and plunged Albania into an economic crisis. They also called for mass protests.

By late Wednesday afternoon the situation was peaceful and most demonstrators had dispersed, leaving a small group of diehards outside Sude's home. A police officer, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Sude faced arrest.
The collapse of her scheme followed the demise of a similar company late last year. Four others have suspended repayments to investors.
The International Monetary Fund and the World Bank have both expressed concern at the spread of the shemes but the government has been slow to act against them.
